short: The Ninth Circuit's August 2026 Amazon v. Perplexity ruling on whether AI agents "access" third-party websites under the CFAA, and what it means for deploying browsing and shopping agents.
title: Agentic AI and the CFAA
subtitle: Amazon v. Perplexity and Computer Fraud and Abuse Act Liability for AI Agents
body_html:
On this page

  • The question Amazon v. Perplexity answers
  • What the Ninth Circuit held
  • What the ruling does not decide
  • Why agentic AI and the CFAA matters to you
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

On August 4, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated a preliminary injunction that had blocked Perplexity's Comet browser agent from shopping Amazon.com on behalf of its users. The panel held that when a user directs an AI agent to act for them, it is the user, not the AI company, who "accesses" the website under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. It is the first federal appellate ruling on agentic AI and the CFAA, and it is deliberately narrow: it decides the CFAA access element for user-directed agents and nothing more. Amazon's trademark and state-law claims are still alive on remand.

The question Amazon v. Perplexity answers

Every company deploying an AI agent that browses, books, buys, or fills forms on a third-party platform has been living with the same unresolved legal question: when the agent touches a website that has told the AI company to stay away, who is doing the touching? If the answer is the AI company, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the federal anti-hacking statute, hangs over every agentic product. If the answer is the user, the agent is legally closer to a web browser than to a bot.

Amazon sued Perplexity over Comet, an AI browser whose agent could log into a user's own Amazon account and shop on the user's instructions. Amazon had demanded Perplexity stop, and a district court entered a preliminary injunction blocking the conduct. The Ninth Circuit took the question head on.

What the Ninth Circuit held

The panel vacated the injunction. Its reasoning: when a user tasks the Comet agent with an action on the user's behalf, using the user's own credentials and the user's own account, the access to Amazon's computers is the user's access. The user is entitled to reach their own account, so the CFAA "without authorization" theory against Perplexity fails at the access element. The court expressly tied the holding to the CFAA access element and to the specific, user-directed design of the Comet technology.

What the ruling does not decide

The holding is narrow by design, and the boundaries matter more than the headline. The court did not decide how the CFAA treats more autonomous AI systems that act without a specific user direction. It did not decide whether an agent's conduct can breach a platform's terms of service, and contract claims survive independently of the CFAA. It did not touch Amazon's trademark and state-law claims, which were remanded to the district court and will shape the practical limits of the ruling. A favorable CFAA outcome is not a general license for agents to operate on unwilling platforms.

Why agentic AI and the CFAA matters to you

If your organization builds or procures AI agents that transact on third-party platforms, this is the first federal appellate precedent you can point to, and it is favorable: user-directed agent activity, on the user's own account, is not a CFAA violation by the agent's provider. That materially lowers one class of legal risk for agentic commerce, procurement bots, and browsing assistants.

The discipline the ruling rewards is the one worth operationalizing now: keep the human's instruction at the front of the chain, keep the agent inside the user's own accounts and credentials, and document both. The further an agent drifts from specific user direction toward autonomous operation, the further it drifts from the protection of this holding. And the remanded trademark and state-law claims are the ones to watch: they can produce many of the same practical restrictions the CFAA claim could not.

Frequently asked questions about agentic AI and the CFAA

Does this ruling mean AI agents can ignore a website's terms of service?

No. The ruling decides only the CFAA access element. Contract, trademark, and state-law theories against agent providers remain fully available, and Amazon is pursuing exactly those claims on remand.

Does it cover fully autonomous agents?

No. The court limited the holding to user-directed activity through the Comet browser. How the CFAA treats an agent acting without a specific user instruction is expressly left open.

Which courts does this bind?

The Ninth Circuit, which covers California, Washington, and the other western states where most large platforms are headquartered and litigate. Other circuits may follow it, distinguish it, or split, and a split is what would put the question in front of the Supreme Court.
